state.claim: Even if your mail-in ballot is postmarked prior to the Election day but arrives after the Election day it will be thrown out.

candidates.quote: Thirty-five states require mailed absentee ballots to be received by election officials on or before Election Day, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, a bipartisan organization that tracks state laws and policies. The other 15 states — along with Washington, Guam, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands — generally allow ballots postmarked by Election Day to arrive afterward, usually within a specified number of days.

That's because while the IRS generally considers a return filed on the day it is postmarked, most states require mail-in ballots to arrive by Election Day, regardless of when they were mailed or postmarked. A postmark shows the date your mail was processed, which may not be the day you mailed the ballot.

Those deadlines vary from state to state. In California, for instance, mail-in ballots postmarked by Election Day can arrive as many as seven days afterward and still be counted, according to NCSL. Colorado, by contrast, requires mail-in ballots to be received by 7 p.m. on Election Day. Some states give military and overseas voters additional time for ballots to arrive after Election Day.

Because election officials in many states qualify mail-in ballots based on the postmark date, this new rule causes problems for thousands of eligible voters who rely on mail-in ballots, putting them at risk for having their votes disqualified should their ballots be postmarked past the deadline—despite having mailed them prior to Election Day.

S2.title: USPS postmark rules: What taxpayers, voters should know - CNBC
S2.retrieval_query: For the relevant jurisdiction and election, what is the official deadline for receipt of mail-in ballots, and does a pre-Election Day postmark extend that deadline?

passages.P2:
* Taxpayers who received a filing extension and plan to mail their return can generally meet the Oct. 15 deadline as long as the postmark is applied on or by that date.
* Most states — 35 of them — require mail-in ballots to arrive by Election Day, which falls on Nov. 3.

passages.P3: Bill Oxford | Istock Unreleased | Getty Images
passages.P4: U.S. Postal Service postmark practices that were formalized in a December 2025 rule could mean a longer delay between when something is mailed and when it's postmarked — a distinction that matters for tax returns, mail-in ballots and other time-sensitive documents.
passages.P5: The issue may crop up as two deadlines approach: Oct. 15 for taxpayers who received a six-month extension to file their federal income tax returns, and Nov. 3 for voters casting ballots in the midterm elections.
passages.P6: Taxpayers who mail their return can meet Thursday's deadline by taking it to the post office for a manual postmark. But voters casting ballots by mail for the midterms can't necessarily count on the same rule.
passages.P7: That's because while the IRS generally considers a return filed on the day it is postmarked, most states require mail-in ballots to arrive by Election Day, regardless of when they were mailed or postmarked. A postmark shows the date your mail was processed, which may not be the day you mailed the ballot.
passages.P8: Thirty-five states require mailed absentee ballots to be received by election officials on or before Election Day, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, a bipartisan organization that tracks state laws and policies. The other 15 states — along with Washington, Guam, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands — generally allow ballots postmarked by Election Day to arrive afterward, usually within a specified number of days.
passages.P9: "State laws govern elections for the most part, and every state has chosen a little bit different way of doing things," said Katy Owens Hubler, director of elections and redistricting for the NCSL.
passages.P11: Nearly 48 million voters cast absentee ballots in the 2024 presidential election, representing roughly 30% of the total 158.2 million ballots cast, according to the U.S. Election Assistance Commission. The absentee figure includes mail-in ballots as well as those returned through drop boxes or in person.
passages.P12: About 1.2% of the mail-in ballots cast in 2024 were rejected, according to the commission. Of them, 40.7% were rejected because the signature on the return envelope didn't match the one on file or was incomplete, and 10% were rejected because they lacked any signature. Another 17.8% were rejected because they were not received by the state's deadline.

passages.P2: # HOW RECENT U.S. POSTAL SERVICE RULE CHANGES PUT MAIL VOTERS AT RISK
passages.P3: ## (and What You Can Do to Ensure Your Vote Counts!)
passages.P4: Print This Page as a PDF
passages.P5: ### Mail-in voting is critical to many elderly, disabled, and rural voters, hourly-employees and non-drivers, for whom travel to a polling place on Election Day is challenging or impossible.
passages.P8: The United States Postal Service (USPS) published **a new rule** that took effect on December 24, 2025, stating that mail might not receive a postmark on the same day the Postal Service takes possession of it, i.e., the day you mail it.
passages.P9: Because election officials in many states qualify mail-in ballots based on the postmark date, this new rule causes problems for thousands of eligible voters who rely on mail-in ballots, putting them at risk for having their votes disqualified should their ballots be postmarked past the deadline—despite having mailed them prior to Election Day.
passages.P10: Additionally, delayed postmarking could affect voter registration forms and absentee ballot applications, which also rely on postmark dates to determine whether deadlines are met.
passages.P11: **In all 44 states covered by the National Voter Registration Act** , election officials have to accept voter registration applications postmarked by the deadline, meaning the new rule will affect who gets access to a ballot in the first place.
passages.P12: The USPS claims it isn’t changing its postmark policy, but is instead merely codifying existing practices.
passages.P14: Total Mail Ballots Cast and Counted in 2024 (EAVS)
passages.P16: This rule change goes into effect at a time when mail voting has been under increasing attack. The current administration has called for a complete ban on mail-in ballots and the Supreme Court is preparing to rule on the constitutionality of “grace period” laws that allow states to count ballots that arrive after Election Day. In 2025, four states — Kansas, North Dakota, Utah, and Ohio — eliminated their grace periods.
passages.P17: Mail-in voting has never been more widely used—31% of Americans voted by mail in 2024, and a Pew Research poll found that a 58% majority of Americans favors expanded early voting. During the 2020 general election, at the height of the COVID pandemic, mail-in voting surged in popularity, with 43% of all votes cast by mail. That percentage has fallen, but in 2024 still amounted to a third of all ballots cast.
passages.P19: The stakes are particularly high for elderly voters, voters who do not drive, voters with disabilities, and rural voters because voters in these groups lack easy access to alternatives, such as in‑person voting or ballot drop boxes for mail voting, and to other methods like motor voter and online voter registration to register to vote. If their postmarks are delayed, they likely have no backup options to vote—despite mailing in the same way they used to.
passages.P20: *Even though dropboxes may be permitted in certain states, they are not always required. Always check with your local election authority for details.*
